'''''Orthotrichum lyellii''''', also known as '''Lyell's bristle moss''',<ref name=":0">{{Cite NatureServe | date =2020 | id =2.122448 | title =''Orthotrichum lyellii'' |access-date=2020-03-22}}</ref> is a species of acrocarpous [[moss]] belonging to the family [[Orthotrichaceae]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Draper|first1=I.|last2=Mazimpaka|first2=V.|last3=Albertos|first3=B.|last4=Garilleti|first4=R.|last5=Lara|first5=F.|date=2005-03-01|title=A survey of the epiphytic bryophyte flora of the Rif and Tazzeka Mountains (northern Morocco)|journal=Journal of Bryology|volume=27|issue=1|pages=23–34|doi=10.1179/174328205X40554|s2cid=55322025|issn=0373-6687|citeseerx=10.1.1.531.4144}}</ref> ''O. lyellii'' can be found throughout western North America and Europe.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://species.nbnatlas.org/species/NHMSYS0000310255|title=Orthotrichum lyellii : Lyell's Bristle-moss {{!}} NBN Atlas|website=species.nbnatlas.org|access-date=2020-03-22}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Orthotrichum%20lyellii|title=E-Flora BC Atlas Page|website=linnet.geog.ubc.ca|access-date=2020-03-22}}</ref> It is found most commonly growing epiphytically on a variety of trees, and less commonly on rocks or boulder substrates.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Vitt|first1=Dale|last2=Sargent|first2=Malcolm|last3=Shevock|first3=James|date=2016-12-01|title=Range Extensions for Orthotrichum lyellii, O. papillosum, and O. pylaisii, with Comments on Taxonomic Distinctions|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/312133918|journal=Evansia|volume=33|issue=4|pages=2016–169|doi=10.1639/0747-9859-33.4.169|s2cid=131907293}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Orthotrichum lyellii'' is generally described as forming green and yellow mats, with loose tufts reaching lengths of 3 to 4 cm forming mound-like structures.<ref name=":3" /> Its leaves are sharply pointed with a single costa and lanceolate linear leaf morphology, being very slender and reaching lengths of 2.5 to 6.5 mm.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=50&taxon_id=250061892|title=Orthotrichum lyellii in Bryophyte Flora of North America @ efloras.org|website=www.efloras.org|access-date=2020-03-27}}</ref> Tufts can reach lengths ranging from 10 to 13 cm, and often are found lying prostrate to the ground.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_moss_treatment.pl?taxon=Orthotrichum%20lyellii|title=California Moss eFlora treatment for Orthotrichum lyellii|website=ucjeps.berkeley.edu|access-date=2020-03-28}}</ref> The lamina cells of its leaves are papillose, and the entire leaf surface can often be found dusted with brown asexual propagules ([[Gemma (botany)|gemmae]]) which may help to distinguish it from similar species such as ''[[Orthotrichum papillosum]].''<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/bbs/Activities/mosses/|title=Index of /bbs/Activities/mosses|website=rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk|access-date=2020-03-27}}</ref> Pale-brown or brown rhizoids may be found located at the base of the plant, with amount of branching varying but usually minimal.<ref name=":5" />

== Habitat and distribution ==
Distribution of ''Orthotrichum lyellii'' in North America is primarily restricted to west of the Rocky Mountains, extending from Southeastern Alaska to California.<ref name=":1" /> It can also be found distributed throughout Europe, descending from the United Kingdom to the Mediterranean area of North Africa and  Western Asia.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" /> ''O. lyellii'' distribution is concentrated in coastal temperate rainforests lying closer to sea level.<ref name=":3" />

''O. lyellii'' grows epiphytically on the surfaces of tree trunks and branches; they are more frequently found growing on deciduous trees such as maple, alder and oak, and less commonly on coniferous trees such as spruce and hemlock.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> They can also be found on the rocks or boulders located beneath said trees, although the frequency of this is low.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=123298|title=Orthotrichum in Flora of North America @ efloras.org|website=www.efloras.org|access-date=2020-03-27}}</ref>

== Reproduction ==
Unique to ''O. lyellii'' within its genus is its dioicous sexual condition, meaning it bears its archegonia and antheridia on different plants.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> The male plants can often be identified by their smaller size and are often found as tufts located near female plants.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vitt|first=Dale|date=1968-01-01|title=Sex determination in mosses|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272293514|journal=Michigan Botanist|volume=7|pages=195–203}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> Another distinctive feature of the male plants is the conspicuous bulb-like branches that harbour its reproductive gametophores.<ref name=":1" />

The sporophytic stage is characterized by rare, slightly exserted capsules that are often immersed in the perichaetial leaves.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> The sporangia is distinct with 8 ribs that may run either one half or the entire length of the sporangia.<ref name=":4" /> Like most mosses belonging to the [[Bryopsida]] class, ''O. lyellii'' has white arthrodontous peristome teeth, with 16 teeth being located in both the exostome and endostome.<ref name=":3" /> Similar to many mosses of the [[Orthotrichum]] genus, the calyptra is hairy with straight hairs running its length, often pointed towards its tip.<ref name=":1" />
